summary: Describes how the IPv6 flow label can improve layer 3/4 load distribution and balancing in large server farms. This is informational guidance.

eli5.summary: A sticker on each packet helps the doorman send the same group to the same worker.

questions: use flow label in server farms
how to use flow label in server farms
subtitle: Use IPv6's flow label field to efficiently distribute traffic across servers.

tldr.problem: Layer 3/4 load balancers in server farms must examine transport-layer headers (TCP/UDP ports) to distribute traffic fairly. With IPv6 extension headers and packet fragmentation, finding those headers is slow and complex.
tldr.mechanism: The IPv6 flow label is a 20-bit field at a fixed position in every IPv6 header. Load balancers can hash this field (along with the source address) to route packets to the same server, avoiding the need to parse extension headers or reassemble fragments.
tldr.outcome: Load balancers can route fragmented traffic and traffic with extension headers faster, with less work. As more traffic uses non-zero flow labels, the performance benefit grows progressively.

facts.label: Advantage over ports
facts.value: Present in all fragments, before any extension headers

today: RFC 7098 is Informational and describes how the IPv6 flow label can be used for load balancing. As of publication, few flows set non-zero flow labels, but the mechanism allows progressive adoption: balancers can start using the flow label for flows that have it while falling back to traditional methods for flows with zero labels.

sections.title: The IPv6 Flow Label
sections.content:
The IPv6 flow label is a 20-bit field in the IPv6 header designed to identify related packets belonging to the same flow, such as all packets in a single TCP connection. According to RFC 6437, the flow label should be constant for a given traffic flow and should follow a uniform statistical distribution, making it useful for load balancing.

A key advantage of the flow label is its fixed position in every IPv6 packet. Transport-layer information such as TCP port numbers comes after any IPv6 extension headers (such as routing headers or fragmentation headers), making it hard to find. In fragmented packets, the transport header appears only in the first fragment. The flow label, by contrast, is always present and always at the same location, even in fragmented packets.
sections.eli5: IPv6 packets have a special number (the flow label) that identifies which connection they belong to. It is always in the same place in the packet, unlike port numbers which might be buried deep inside.

sections.title: Load Balancing in Server Farms
sections.content:
Large server farms use load balancers to distribute traffic among multiple servers. Different types of load balancers exist. Layer 7 load balancers (like HTTP reverse proxies) understand the application protocol and can make sophisticated routing decisions but are expensive. Layer 3/4 load balancers operate at the IP and TCP/UDP level, making fast routing decisions based on protocol headers. They may be stateless (hashing each packet independently) or stateful (recording which server each flow is assigned to).

Layer 3/4 load balancers must classify each incoming packet and select a target server while ensuring persistence: all packets from a single client session go to the same server. Traditionally they do this by examining the 5-tuple (source address, destination address, protocol, source port, destination port) and hashing it to select a server. However, finding the port numbers requires parsing through extension headers.
sections.eli5: A load balancer is a traffic director at a server farm. It looks at incoming packets and decides which server should handle them, making sure all packets from the same person go to the same server.

sections.title: Using the Flow Label for Layer 3/4 Load Balancing
sections.content:
When a packet has a non-zero flow label set according to RFC 6437, a layer 3/4 load balancer can use the 2-tuple {source address, flow label} as the session key for load distribution, or optionally the 3-tuple {destination address, source address, flow label}. The balancer can hash this tuple to select a server consistently for the flow.

The benefit is clear: no need to parse extension headers to find port numbers, and fragmented packets work fine because the flow label is in every fragment. A stateless balancer can apply the same hash algorithm to all packets. A stateful balancer can store the {tuple, server} association on the first packet and use the stored mapping for all subsequent packets of the same flow.

For backward compatibility, if the flow label is zero, the balancer falls back to traditional port-based hashing. As IPv6 implementations increasingly set non-zero flow labels, the performance benefit of this approach grows progressively.
sections.eli5: If the flow label is set, the balancer can use it like a pre-computed label: just hash it with the source address and send the packet to the server that hash points to. No need to dig for port numbers, so it is faster, especially for packets that are broken into pieces.

sections.title: Implementation Details and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC notes several considerations. The flow label is only 20 bits, so there are about one million possible values. If two simultaneous flows from the same source address happen to have the same flow label (a rare statistical event), both flows would be assigned to the same server. They would then be distinguished by their port numbers on the server. With a million possible label values, it is unlikely there will be more flow labels than servers at most sites, so this collision risk is acceptable.

A stateful load balancer using the flow label will not detect the end of sessions by watching for TCP FIN/ACK sequences, since it avoids parsing the transport layer. Instead, it relies on inactivity timers to clean up session state, a technique all load balancers already use for hung sessions.

Load balancers that use Network Address Port Translation (NAPT) to rewrite the destination address and port must still parse extension headers to modify the port and checksum, so they see no performance benefit from the flow label. Similarly, balancers that perform TCP state tracking must always look at the transport layer.
sections.eli5: Sometimes two different connections might get the same label by chance, but it is so rare that it does not matter. The server will sort them out using the actual port numbers. The balancer will not notice when connections end, so it uses timers to clean up old connections, just like balancers do today.
